metadata.chapter_title: Linear Inequalities, Simultaneous Equations, and Coordinate Geometry
metadata.title: Solving Linear Inequalities and Half-Planes
metadata.vcaa_description: Solve linear inequalities and simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables; interpret solutions graphically and apply to real-world contexts.
metadata.target_mastery: Solve linear inequalities (reversing the inequality sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative), graph solution sets on a number line, and shade half-planes.

key_vocabulary.definition: A mathematical statement comparing two linear expressions using an inequality symbol ($<$, $>$, $\le$, or $\ge$).

A strict inequality ($<$ or $>$) excludes the boundary value (drawn with an open circle or dashed boundary line), whereas an inclusive inequality ($\le$ or $\ge$) includes the boundary value (closed circle or solid line).
Two inequalities joined into a single three-part statement, such as $-3 \le 2x + 1 < 7$, defining a bounded interval on the real number line.
The region of the Cartesian plane lying on one side of a boundary straight line $ax + by = c$, representing all points $(x, y)$ that satisfy a two-variable linear inequality.

theory.title: Properties of Inequalities and Reversing the Sign
theory.explanation: Solving a linear inequality in one variable uses the same inverse operations as solving a linear equation, with one critical exception: multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the order of the real number line, so the inequality symbol must be flipped ($<$ becomes $>$, and $\le$ becomes $\ge$). Adding or subtracting any number, or multiplying/dividing by a positive number, leaves the inequality symbol unchanged.
theory.formula_latex: \text{If } a < b \text{ and } c < 0, \text{ then } ac > bc \text{ and } \frac{a}{c} > \frac{b}{c}
theory.callout_title: Multiply or Divide by a Negative? Flip the Sign!
theory.callout_rule: Notice that $2 < 5$, but multiplying both sides by $-1$ gives $-2 > -5$. Whenever the coefficient of $x$ that you divide by is negative, reverse the inequality direction immediately.

theory.title: Number Line Graphs and Compound Inequalities
theory.explanation: The solution set of a one-variable linear inequality is an infinite interval of real numbers. On a number line, an open circle ($\circ$) at $a$ indicates that $a$ is excluded ($x < a$ or $x > a$), while a filled/closed circle ($\bullet$) indicates that $a$ is included ($x \le a$ or $x \ge a$). A three-part compound inequality $a \le mx + c < b$ is solved by performing the same inverse operations on all three parts simultaneously.
theory.formula_latex: a \le mx + c < b \iff \frac{a - c}{m} \le x < \frac{b - c}{m} \quad (m > 0)
theory.callout_title: Apply Every Operation to All Three Parts
theory.callout_rule: When solving $-5 < 2x - 1 \le 7$, add $1$ to the left, middle, AND right parts ($-4 < 2x \le 8$), then divide all three parts by $2$ ($-2 < x \le 4$).

theory.title: Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables (Half-Planes)
theory.explanation: A linear inequality in two variables, such as $y \le 2x + 3$ or $2x + 3y > 6$, divides the Cartesian plane into two half-planes separated by the boundary line $y = 2x + 3$ or $2x + 3y = 6$. Draw the boundary line as a dashed line for strict inequalities ($<$ or $>$) or a solid line for inclusive inequalities ($\le$ or $\ge$). Then substitute a convenient test point not on the line—usually the origin $(0, 0)$—to determine which half-plane satisfies the inequality.
theory.formula_latex: y > mx + c \text{ (above dashed line)}, \quad y \le mx + c \text{ (on or below solid line)}
theory.callout_title: Test the Origin $(0, 0)$ to Pick the Correct Half-Plane
theory.callout_rule: If the boundary line does not pass through $(0, 0)$, substitute $x = 0, y = 0$ into the inequality. If the statement is true, $(0, 0)$ lies in the required region; if false, the required region is on the opposite side of the line.

worked_examples.title: Solving a Linear Inequality with a Negative Coefficient
worked_examples.problem: Solve the inequality $7 - 3x \ge 19$ and describe its graph on a number line.

steps.thinking: Subtract $7$ from both sides of the inequality (this does not change the inequality direction).
Divide both sides by $-3$ and reverse the inequality sign from $\ge$ to $\le$.

steps.working: $$\text{Closed circle at } x = -4 \text{ with an arrow pointing left.}$$

now_you_try.hint: Subtract $11$ first, then divide by $-4$ and flip the $<$ sign to $>$.

worked_examples.title: Solving a Three-Part Compound Inequality
worked_examples.problem: Solve the compound inequality $-5 \le 2x + 3 < 11$ and list all integer values of $x$ that satisfy it.

steps.thinking: Subtract $3$ from all three parts of the compound inequality.
Divide all three parts by $+2$ (positive, so the inequality signs remain in the same direction).
List the integers from $-4$ (inclusive) up to $4$ (strictly excluded).

now_you_try.hint: Add $1$ to all three parts, then divide all three parts by $3$.

worked_examples.title: Identifying a Half-Plane Using Intercepts and a Test Point
worked_examples.problem: Describe how to sketch the half-plane defined by $2x + 3y < 12$, including the boundary line type, axis intercepts, and whether the origin $(0, 0)$ is included in the solution region.

steps.thinking: Find the axis intercepts of the boundary line $2x + 3y = 12$ by setting $y = 0$ and $x = 0$.
Because the inequality $<$ is strict, the boundary line through $(6, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$ is drawn dashed.

steps.working: $$0 < 12 \text{ (True)} \implies \text{the half-plane containing } (0, 0) \text{ below the line is the solution region.}$$

worked_examples.final_answer: Dashed line through $(6, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$; the region below the line containing $(0, 0)$

now_you_try.problem: Find the axis intercepts of the boundary line for $4x - y \ge 8$ and determine whether $(0, 0)$ satisfies the inequality.
now_you_try.hint: Substitute $(0, 0)$ into $4x - y \ge 8$ to check whether $0 \ge 8$ is true or false.
now_you_try.working_summary: Intercepts $(2, 0)$ and $(0, -8)$ (solid line); at $(0, 0)$, $0 \ge 8$ is false, so $(0, 0)$ is NOT in the region.
now_you_try.answer: Solid line through $(2, 0)$ and $(0, -8)$; $(0, 0)$ does not satisfy the inequality

common_misconceptions.title: Flipping the Inequality Sign Whenever a Negative Number Appears on the Right-Hand Side
common_misconceptions.misconception: Reversing the inequality sign when solving $2x < -10$ to get $x > -5$, simply because $-10$ is negative.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: The inequality sign reverses ONLY when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number. In $2x < -10$, you divide by $+2$ (which is positive), so the sign stays $<$: $x < -5$.

common_misconceptions.title: Using a Solid Boundary Line for a Strict Inequality
common_misconceptions.misconception: Drawing a solid boundary line for $y > 2x - 1$ instead of a dashed line.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Points on the line $y = 2x - 1$ make the two sides equal, so they do NOT satisfy the strict inequality $y > 2x - 1$. A dashed line visually communicates that points on the boundary are excluded.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: The point $(1, 1)$ lies on the boundary line $y = 2x - 1$, and substituting $(1, 1)$ into $y > 2x - 1$ gives $1 > 1$, which is false.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Solve the linear inequality $5x - 8 > 2x + 7$.
step_by_step_solution: Subtract $2x$ from both sides and add $8$ to both sides: $3x > 15$.
Divide both sides by $3$: $x > 5$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Solve the linear inequality $4(2 - x) \le 20$.
step_by_step_solution: Divide both sides by $4$: $2 - x \le 5$.
Subtract $2$ from both sides: $-x \le 3$. Multiply by $-1$ and flip the sign: $x \ge -3$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Solve the fractional inequality $\frac{3 - 2x}{5} > -1$.
step_by_step_solution: Multiply both sides by $+5$: $3 - 2x > -5$.
Subtract $3$ from both sides: $-2x > -8$.
Divide by $-2$ and reverse the inequality sign: $x < 4$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Solve the compound inequality $-3 \le \frac{4x - 2}{2} < 5$.
step_by_step_solution: Multiply all three parts by $2$: $-6 \le 4x - 2 < 10$.
Add $2$ to all three parts: $-4 \le 4x < 12$.
Divide all three parts by $4$: $-1 \le x < 3$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A Ballarat plumber charges a $\$90$ call-out fee plus $\$65$ per hour. If a homeowner has a maximum budget of $\$350$, write and solve a linear inequality to find the maximum number of hours $h$ the plumber can work.
step_by_step_solution: Set up the inequality: $65h + 90 \le 350$.
Subtract $90$: $65h \le 260$.
Divide by $65$: $h \le 4\text{ hours}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: Amira scored $74$, $81$, and $79$ on her first three Year 10 Mathematics tests. What minimum score $x$ must she achieve on her fourth test to have an average of at least $80$ across all four tests?
step_by_step_solution: Write the average inequality: $\frac{74 + 81 + 79 + x}{4} \ge 80$.
Multiply both sides by $4$: $234 + x \ge 320$.
Subtract $234$: $x \ge 86$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A school drama production sells student tickets for $\$10$ ($x$) and adult tickets for $\$25$ ($y$). To cover hall hire costs, total revenue must be at least $\$500$. Write a two-variable inequality modelling this requirement and determine whether selling $18$ student tickets and $12$ adult tickets meets the target.
problem_solving_and_modelling.final_answer: $10x + 25y \ge 500$; yes, since $10(18) + 25(12) = \$480 < \$500$ is false—actually $\$480$ is $\$20$ short, so it does NOT meet the target
step_by_step_solution: The revenue inequality is $10x + 25y \ge 500$ (where $x, y \ge 0$ are integers).
Since $480 < 500$, the point $(18, 12)$ does not satisfy $10x + 25y \ge 500$ ($\$20$ short of the target).

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A triangle in the first quadrant is bounded by $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, and $3x + 4y \le 12$. Find the vertices of this triangular region and calculate its exact area.
step_by_step_solution: The boundary line $3x + 4y = 12$ meets the $x$-axis ($y = 0$) at $(4, 0)$ and the $y$-axis ($x = 0$) at $(0, 3)$.
With $x \ge 0$ and $y \ge 0$, the region is a right-angled triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, and $(0, 3)$.
Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3 = 6\text{ square units}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Use subtraction to prove algebraically why $a < b$ implies $-a > -b$ for any real numbers $a$ and $b$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Subtracting $(a + b)$ from both sides of $a < b$ preserves the inequality direction and yields $-b < -a$, i.e. $-a > -b$
step_by_step_solution: Start with $a < b$. Adding or subtracting any real number from both sides preserves the inequality order.
Subtract $a$ from both sides: $0 < b - a$.
Subtract $b$ from both sides: $-b < -a$, which is identical to $-a > -b$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Explain why the test point $(0, 0)$ cannot be used to decide which side of the boundary line $y \ge 3x$ to shade, and choose a valid alternative test point to determine the correct half-plane.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: $(0, 0)$ lies on the boundary line $y = 3x$; testing $(1, 0)$ gives $0 \ge 3$ (False), so shade the half-plane above/left of $y = 3x$
step_by_step_solution: When $x = 0$ and $y = 0$, $0 = 3(0)$, so $(0, 0)$ lies directly ON the boundary line $y = 3x$ and cannot distinguish between the two open half-planes.
Choose a point not on the line, such as $(1, 0)$: substituting into $y \ge 3x$ gives $0 \ge 3$ (False), so we shade the opposite side (containing $(0, 1)$, where $1 \ge 0$ is True).

reasoning_and_communication.question: Find all values of $x$ that satisfy BOTH $3x - 5 < 10$ and $1 - 2x \le 7$, and state the number of integers in the intersection.
step_by_step_solution: Solve the first inequality: $3x < 15 \implies x < 5$.
Solve the second inequality: $-2x \le 6 \implies x \ge -3$.
Combining both gives $-3 \le x < 5$, which contains the $8$ integers $\{-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: A student attempts to solve $\frac{6}{x} < 2$ by multiplying both sides by $x$ to write $6 < 2x \implies x > 3$. Explain why this method misses an entire interval of solutions, and state the complete solution set.
reasoning_and_communication.context: Sign of Unknown Variable in Denominator
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: If $x < 0$, multiplying by $x$ reverses the inequality sign (and $\frac{6}{x}$ is negative, which is always $< 2$); complete solution is $x < 0$ or $x > 3$
step_by_step_solution: Because the sign of $x$ is unknown, multiplying by $x$ is only valid without flipping the sign when $x > 0$ (which gives $x > 3$).
Whenever $x < 0$, the left-hand side $\frac{6}{x}$ is negative and therefore automatically less than $+2$, so the complete solution is $x < 0$ or $x > 3$.
